label: Steps a day
body:
Heart and longevity benefits climb
steeply up to about 8,000 steps.
No gym needed. A 10-min walk after
meals also blunts sugar spikes.
caption:
You don't need 10,000 steps. But you probably need more than you're doing.

The 10k number came from a 1960s pedometer ad — not science.

What large studies actually show: the risk of early death drops steeply as daily steps rise, and the benefit starts levelling off around 7,000–8,000 steps for most adults.

Easy ways to get there:
→ 10-minute walk after each meal
→ Take calls standing or walking
→ Stairs instead of the lift
→ Park or get off one stop early

Walking is the most underrated health habit there is.

Vitamin D

India gets more sunshine than most countries. So why are most Indians low on vitamin D?

→ 15–20 min of midday sun on arms and legs, a few times a week

Fruit juice is
healthy?

That "100% natural" juice box isn't the health drink it looks like.

Juicing strips out the fibre — the part that slows sugar down.

What happens without the fibre:
→ Sugar hits your blood fast
→ You're hungry again soon
→ It's easy to drink 3 oranges' worth in 30 seconds

Sleeping badly even though you're exhausted? Check when you had your last chai.

→ Reduces deep sleep
→ Makes sleep lighter and more broken
→ Leaves you groggy the next morning
→ So you reach for more caffeine… and repeat

Veg diet covers

Vitamin B12.

→ Stronger bones and joints
→ Better blood sugar control
→ Higher resting metabolism

label: Did you know
headline:
Rest days
build muscle.

Training hard every single day and not seeing results? You might need less, not more.

Skip recovery and you get:
→ Stalled strength
→ Constant soreness
→ Poor sleep and low energy
→ Higher injury risk

The rule of thumb: about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Walking and stretching on rest days is great.

→ 10 minutes of morning sunlight

label: Did you know
headline:
Your resting
heart rate talks.
body: Normal is 60–100 bpm, and fitter people sit lower. If yours stays higher than usual for days, it can signal poor sleep, stress or illness.
caption:
Your resting heart rate is one of the simplest health signals you can track — and it's free.

Measure it in the morning, before getting out of bed.

What the numbers mean:
→ 60–100 bpm is the normal adult range
→ Regular exercise usually brings it lower over time
→ A rise of several beats for days can mean poor sleep, stress, dehydration or an oncoming illness

Track it for a week to learn your baseline. Changes matter more than one reading.

label: Healthy blood pressure
body:
Below 120/80 mmHg is ideal.
140/90 or above on repeat checks
is high BP. It rarely has symptoms,
so the only way to know is to check.
caption:
High blood pressure is called the silent killer for a reason. Most people with it feel completely fine.

Until a heart attack or stroke.

What the numbers mean:
→ Below 120/80 — ideal
→ 120–139 / 80–89 — higher than ideal, time to act
→ 140/90 or above on repeat readings — high blood pressure

What brings it down:
→ Less salt (pickles, papad, namkeen, packaged food)
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Losing even a few kg if you're overweight
→ Less alcohol, no smoking

Every adult should know their number. Get it checked at least once a year.

label: Wellbeing
headline:
Breathe out
the stress
body: Breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6. A longer exhale slows your heart rate and calms you down. Five minutes is enough.
caption:
Feeling wound up before a meeting, an exam or a tough conversation? Your breath is the fastest off-switch you have.

And it's free.

When you breathe out slowly, your heart rate drops a little and your body shifts out of "fight or flight".

Try it right now:
→ Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts
→ Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 6 counts
→ Keep your shoulders relaxed
→ Repeat for 5 minutes

Eating late
makes you fat?

"Don't eat after 7 PM or you'll gain weight." Heard this one?

Your body doesn't have a clock that turns food into fat after sunset.

Weight change comes from your total calories over days and weeks — not the time on the clock.

Why late eating gets the blame:
→ Late-night snacking is usually extra food, not a meal
→ It's often chips, sweets and biscuits
→ A heavy dinner right before bed can cause acidity and poor sleep
→ Poor sleep makes you hungrier the next day

The smart move: eat dinner 2–3 hours before bed and keep it balanced. If you're truly hungry later, curd, fruit or a handful of nuts.

How many teaspoons of sugar do you have a day? Most people have no idea.

→ Chai and coffee (2 tsp a cup adds up fast)
→ Biscuits, rusks and "healthy" cereals

→ Ketchup, sauces and flavoured yoghurt

→ Reduce sugar in chai by half a spoon every week
→ Swap biscuits for fruit or nuts
→ Water or chaas instead of cold drinks

label: Reality check
headline:
Multigrain means
healthy?
body: Many multigrain breads and biscuits are mostly maida with a sprinkle of other grains. Check the ingredients list — the first item is the main one.
caption:
"Multigrain" on the pack sounds healthy. But it doesn't mean whole grain.

It just means more than one grain is in there — even if it's a tiny amount.

Many multigrain breads, biscuits and atta blends are mostly refined flour (maida) with a little oats, ragi or flax added for the label.

How to check in 10 seconds:
→ Read the ingredients list — they're listed from most to least
→ First ingredient should be "whole wheat" or another whole grain
→ "Wheat flour" or "refined wheat flour" usually means maida
→ Compare fibre: aim for 6 g or more per 100 g

Trust the ingredients, not the front of the pack.

→ Full push-ups

Move to the next level when you can do 3 clean sets of 10.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your ears clean
themselves.
body: Ear wax moves out on its own as you chew and talk. Cotton buds push it deeper and can hurt your eardrum. Just wipe the outer ear.
caption:
Cleaning your ears with cotton buds every day? You're probably doing more harm than good.

Ear wax isn't dirt. It traps dust, keeps the ear canal moist and helps fight infection.

Your ears are self-cleaning: jaw movement slowly pushes old wax outwards.

What cotton buds actually do:
→ Push wax deeper, causing blockages
→ Scratch the delicate skin of the ear canal
→ Can damage your eardrum

What to do instead:
→ Wipe the outer ear with a cloth after a bath
→ Never put hairpins, keys or oil drops inside
→ See a doctor for pain, blocked hearing or discharge

Leave your ears alone. They've got this.

label: HbA1c warning line
body:
HbA1c shows your average sugar
over the last 2–3 months.
Below 5.7% normal. 5.7–6.4%
prediabetes. 6.5%+ diabetes.
caption:
A fasting sugar test shows one morning. HbA1c shows the last 2–3 months.

That's why doctors trust it.

HbA1c measures how much sugar has stuck to your red blood cells, which live about 3 months.

What the result means:
→ Below 5.7% — normal
→ 5.7% to 6.4% — prediabetes
→ 6.5% or higher — diabetes (confirmed by your doctor)

Prediabetes is the window where lifestyle changes work best:
→ Lose 5–7% of your body weight if overweight
→ 150 minutes of activity a week
→ Fewer refined carbs and sugary drinks

Over 30, or diabetes in the family? Ask for an HbA1c test.

headline:
Heart attack
warning signs

sections.title: Chest
sections.text: Pressure, squeezing or pain lasting minutes.

sections.title: Spreading
sections.text: To the arm, jaw, neck or back.

sections.title: With
sections.text: Breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea.

caption:
Knowing these signs can save a life — maybe someone at home.

In a heart attack, every minute matters.

Common warning signs:
→ Chest pressure, squeezing or pain that lasts more than a few minutes
→ Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck, back or upper stomach
→ Shortness of breath
→ Cold sweat, nausea or light-headedness

Women, older people and people with diabetes often have milder or unusual symptoms — like only breathlessness, tiredness or "gas".

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112 straight away
→ Don't drive yourself to hospital
→ Don't wait to "see if it passes"

Carbs make

caption:
Rice, roti and fruit aren't the enemy. Cutting all carbs isn't the secret to fat loss.

Weight gain comes from eating more calories than you use — whether they come from carbs, fat or protein.

→ Huge portions of white rice or maida
→ Sugary drinks, sweets and biscuits
→ Fried snacks (carbs + oil = easy to overeat)
→ Carbs with almost no protein or vegetables

→ Dal, rajma, chana
→ Fruit and vegetables
→ Millets, oats, whole wheat roti

The fix isn't zero carbs. It's better carbs, sensible portions, and protein on the plate.

caption:
Your waist size may say more about your health than your weight does.

That fat is linked to diabetes, heart disease and fatty liver.

→ Stand straight and breathe out normally

→ Tape snug, not pressing into the skin

Curd for

Curd (dahi).

Tea with meals
blocks iron.
body: Tannins in tea and coffee cut how much iron you absorb from food. Keep a one-hour gap. Pair dal or greens with lemon or amla instead.
caption:
Chai right after lunch is a habit for many of us. It may be costing you iron.

Tea and coffee contain tannins and polyphenols. They bind to the iron in plant foods and reduce how much your body absorbs.

This matters a lot in India, where anaemia is very common — especially in women.

→ Keep a gap of about an hour between meals and chai or coffee
→ Add vitamin C to iron-rich meals: lemon, amla, guava, tomato
→ Eat iron-rich foods: dal, chana, rajma, green leafy veg, ragi

label: Safe level of alcohol

for health. Risk of cancer and
other harm starts from the first
drink and rises with every one.

"A drink a day is good for the heart." That idea hasn't held up.

Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen — the same category as tobacco.

→ At least 7 types of cancer, including breast and bowel
→ High blood pressure and heart rhythm problems
→ Fatty liver and liver disease
→ Poor sleep, weight gain and low mood

If you drink:
→ Less is always better
→ Have alcohol-free days every week
→ Never drink and drive

label: Sleep
headline:
Can't sleep?
Get up.
body: Lying awake teaches your brain that bed means stress. Get up, sit somewhere dim and calm, and go back only when you're sleepy.
caption:
Tossing and turning for an hour? Staying in bed is making it worse.

When you lie awake night after night, your brain starts linking your bed with frustration, not sleep.

Sleep doctors use a simple rule:
→ If you're awake for about 20 minutes, get out of bed
→ Sit somewhere dim and quiet
→ Read a paper book or listen to something calm — no phone
→ Go back to bed only when you feel sleepy
→ Repeat if needed

Also: keep the same wake-up time, even after a bad night.

Sweating more

body: Sweat is how your body cools down, not how it burns fat. The weight you lose is water, and it comes back as soon as you drink.
caption:
Wearing a sweat suit or working out in a hot room to "melt the fat"? It doesn't work like that.

Sweat is water your body releases to cool down.

How much you sweat depends on heat, humidity, genetics and fitness — not on how much fat you're burning.

What really happens:
→ You lose water weight
→ The scale drops for a few hours
→ You drink water, and it comes right back
→ Too much sweating can leave you dehydrated and dizzy

What does burn fat: a consistent calorie deficit, strength training, daily movement and enough protein.

label: BMI cutoff for Indians
body:
For Asian Indians, BMI 23–24.9
counts as overweight, 25+ as obese.
The global cutoffs (25/30) miss
risk that starts earlier for us.
caption:
Your BMI says "normal"? For Indians, the usual chart can be misleading.

Asian Indians tend to develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations.

That's why Indian guidelines use lower cutoffs:
→ 18.5–22.9 — normal
→ 23–24.9 — overweight
→ 25 and above — obese

How to calculate: weight (kg) ÷ height (m) ÷ height (m).

label: Reality check
headline:
Protein bars are
health food?
body: Many protein bars carry as much sugar and calories as a chocolate bar. Check the label. A handful of nuts, chana or curd often does better.
caption:
That protein bar in your gym bag might be a chocolate bar in disguise.

Many popular bars contain:
→ 10–20 g of sugar or syrups
→ 200–300 calories
→ Less protein than the front of the pack suggests
→ Sugar alcohols that can cause bloating

Your bones
are alive.

Bones aren't dead scaffolding. They're living tissue that rebuilds itself every day.

Your body is always breaking down old bone and laying down new bone.

→ Strength training and impact (walking, stairs, skipping)

→ Vitamin D from sunlight (and testing if you're low)

caption:
Tuition, homework, screens — where's the time to play? Children need it more than ever.

WHO recommends that children and teens aged 5–17 get at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day.

What counts:
→ Running, cycling, skipping
→ Football, cricket, badminton, kabaddi
→ Dancing, swimming
→ Brisk walking to school

At least 3 days a week should include activities that strengthen muscles and bones, like jumping and climbing.

Why it matters:
→ Better focus and grades
→ Stronger bones and heart
→ Better sleep and mood
→ Lower risk of childhood obesity

Play is not a waste of time.

Running ruins

"Don't run, you'll ruin your knees." It's one of the most common warnings — and the evidence doesn't back it up.

→ Doing too much too soon
→ Weak hips and thighs
→ Running through sharp pain
→ Carrying a lot of extra weight

label: Fever starts here
body:
A temperature of 38°C (100.4°F)
or higher counts as a fever.
Rest and fluids help. See a doctor
if it lasts 3 days or is very high.
caption:
Feeling warm? A thermometer settles it. Not every warm forehead is a fever.

Normal body temperature is around 37°C (98.6°F), and it changes a little through the day.

A fever is usually 38°C (100.4°F) or higher.

What helps at home:
→ Rest
→ Plenty of fluids — water, ORS, soups, coconut water
→ Light clothing and a cool room

See a doctor if:
→ Fever lasts more than 3 days
→ It's 39.4°C (103°F) or higher
→ There's a rash, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or trouble breathing
→ It's an infant, older person, or someone with a long-term illness

During dengue season, don't ignore a fever.

Weekend lie-ins
fix sleep debt?

Five short nights, then sleeping till noon on Sunday? That's not catching up — it's jet lag at home.

Extra sleep at the weekend can ease some tiredness. But it doesn't fully undo a week of short sleep.

And a big shift in your wake time confuses your body clock. Scientists call it "social jet lag".

→ Hard to fall asleep on Sunday night
→ Groggy Monday mornings
→ More cravings and lower mood

A better plan:
→ Keep weekend wake time within an hour of weekdays
→ Take a short afternoon nap if you need it
→ Fix weekday sleep, rather than repaying it later

Consistency beats catch-up.

Beat
constipation

→ Sitting all day
→ Ignoring the urge to go

After an 8-hour fast:
Under 100 mg/dL is normal.

126 or more on 2 tests: diabetes.

A fasting blood sugar test is cheap, quick and tells you a lot.

→ Below 100 mg/dL — normal
→ 100 to 125 mg/dL — prediabetes

→ Daily walking and strength training
→ Less sugar and refined carbs
→ More protein, fibre and vegetables
→ Losing weight if you carry extra around the waist

A good warm-up takes just 5–10 minutes and makes your workout safer and better.

→ Raises your body temperature and heart rate
→ Gets your joints moving freely
→ Wakes up the muscles you're about to use

→ 3–5 minutes of brisk walking, light jogging or skipping
→ Arm circles, leg swings, hip circles, bodyweight squats
→ 1–2 lighter sets of your first exercise

label: Myth buster
headline:
No pain,
no gain?
body: Effort should feel hard, but pain is a warning. Sharp, sudden or joint pain means stop. Progress comes from steady effort over months.
caption:
"No pain, no gain" sounds tough. It also causes a lot of injuries.

There's a big difference between effort and pain.

Normal (keep going):
→ Muscles burning near the end of a set
→ Heavy breathing during cardio
→ Mild soreness 1–2 days later

Warning signs (stop):
→ Sharp or stabbing pain
→ Pain in a joint, not a muscle
→ Pain that gets worse as you continue
→ Swelling, or pain that lasts more than a few days

Results come from training consistently for months — not from destroying yourself in one session.

label: Days to a habit

Not 21. In one study, new habits
took 66 days on average to stick —
from 18 to 254 days. Missing
a day now and then is fine.
caption:
"It takes 21 days to build a habit." That number has no real science behind it.

A University College London study followed people building new daily habits, like drinking water with lunch or going for a run.

On average, it took 66 days for a habit to become automatic. Some took 18 days, others more than 250.

The good news:
→ Missing a single day didn't derail the habit
→ Simple habits stuck faster than complex ones

How to make habits stick:
→ Start tiny (2 push-ups, not 50)
→ Tie it to something you already do ("after brushing, I…")
→ Same time, same place
→ Track it on a calendar

Give it two months, not three weeks.

Herbal means

"It's herbal, so it can't harm." Many people think this. It isn't always true.

Plants contain active compounds — that's why some work. It's also why they can cause problems.

→ Interactions with blood thinners, diabetes or BP medicines
→ Liver damage with some concentrated extracts
→ Contamination or wrong doses in poorly made products
→ Stopping prescribed medicine because a supplement "will do"

Stay safe:
→ Buy from trusted, licensed brands
→ Tell your doctor about every supplement, powder or kadha you take regularly
→ Never stop prescribed medicine without advice
→ Be wary of anything promising a "cure"

Your gut and
brain talk.

Ever had butterflies before a big moment, or needed the toilet before an exam? That's your gut-brain connection.

→ Gut problems can affect your mood and energy
→ IBS symptoms often get worse with stress

WHO: breast milk alone for the
first 6 months — no water, honey
or ghutti. Then add solid foods
and continue to 2 years or beyond.

For a baby's first six months, breast milk is all they need. Not even water.

WHO and UNICEF recommend:
→ Starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth
→ Only breast milk for the first 6 months
→ Adding safe, nutritious solid foods from 6 months
→ Continuing breastfeeding up to 2 years or beyond

→ Water, even in summer (breast milk is mostly water)
→ Honey, ghutti or janam ghutti
→ Animal milk or other drinks

Breastfeeding protects babies against infections and benefits mothers too.

label: Women's health

PCOS: the
basics
body: Irregular periods, acne, extra hair and weight gain are common signs. Losing even 5–10% of body weight can improve cycles and symptoms.
caption:
PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is one of the most common hormone conditions in women of reproductive age.

Common signs:
→ Irregular or missed periods
→ Acne and oily skin
→ Extra hair on the face or body
→ Weight gain, especially around the belly
→ Thinning hair on the scalp

PCOS is closely linked to insulin resistance, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes later.

What helps most people:
→ Losing 5–10% of body weight, if overweight
→ Strength training and daily walking
→ Protein and fibre in every meal, fewer refined carbs
→ Regular sleep

If you think you have PCOS, see a gynaecologist. Treatment is available.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Cold water after
meals = fat?
body: Cold water does not turn food into fat or "freeze" it in your stomach. Drink water at whatever temperature you like, with or after meals.
caption:
"Never drink cold water after eating — it solidifies the fat." This one gets forwarded a lot.

It isn't true.

Your stomach quickly brings any drink to body temperature. Cold water doesn't make food harder to digest, and it doesn't cause weight gain.

What's true:
→ Water with meals is fine and can help you feel full
→ Warm water may feel more soothing to some people — that's preference
→ Some people with certain throat or oesophagus conditions find cold drinks uncomfortable

What matters more for digestion:
→ Eating slowly
→ Fibre and enough water through the day
→ Not lying down right after a big meal

Drink water. Any temperature.

label: Indians with fatty liver
body:
Studies estimate about 1 in 3
Indian adults has fatty liver,
often with no symptoms — even at
a normal weight. It is reversible.
caption:
Fatty liver is far more common than most people realise — and it usually has no symptoms.

Studies estimate that about 1 in 3 Indian adults has non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, where fat builds up in the liver.

Who's at higher risk:
→ People with a large waist or excess weight
→ People with diabetes or prediabetes
→ High triglycerides
→ Even "thin" people with belly fat

Left unchecked, it can lead to liver inflammation and scarring.

The good news — it's often reversible:
→ Losing 7–10% of body weight can reduce liver fat significantly
→ Daily activity
→ Cut sugary drinks, sweets and refined carbs
→ Avoid alcohol

Ask your doctor about a liver check if you're at risk.

label: Reality check

Thyroid is why
you gain weight?
body: An underactive thyroid can add a few kilos, often fluid. Once treated, it shouldn't block fat loss. Get tested, then focus on habits.
caption:
"I can't lose weight because of my thyroid." Sometimes there's some truth to it — but usually less than people think.

Hypothyroidism (an underactive thyroid) slows metabolism and can cause modest weight gain, partly from fluid.

Once it's diagnosed and treated, thyroid levels return to normal — and weight loss works the same way as for anyone else.

Signs worth testing for:
→ Tiredness and feeling cold
→ Dry skin and hair fall
→ Constipation
→ Irregular periods
→ Unexplained weight gain

What to do:
→ Get a TSH test
→ Take medicine exactly as prescribed
→ Then focus on food, movement and sleep

Your thyroid isn't a life sentence for weight.

label: Did you know
headline:
One-leg balance
predicts health.
body: In a large study of middle-aged and older adults, those who could not stand on one leg for 10 seconds had a higher risk of dying earlier.

Can you stand on one leg for 10 seconds? It's a simple test with a surprising link to health.

A 2022 study followed over 1,700 adults aged 51–75. Those who couldn't balance on one leg for 10 seconds were significantly more likely to die over the next 7 years than those who could.

Balance reflects strength, coordination and overall fitness — and it declines with age if not used.

Try it (near a wall for safety):
→ Stand on one foot, other foot resting behind the standing leg
→ Arms by your sides, eyes forward
→ Aim for 10 seconds on each leg

label: Total cholesterol

Total under 200. LDL under 100.
HDL over 40 (men), 50 (women).

Got a lipid profile report and not sure what it means? Here's a quick guide.

Typical healthy targets (mg/dL):
→ Total cholesterol: below 200
→ LDL ("bad"): below 100 — lower if your doctor advises
→ HDL ("good"): above 40 for men, above 50 for women
→ Triglycerides: below 150

What helps:
→ Cut trans fats (vanaspati, bakery and fried snacks)
→ More fibre — oats, dal, fruit, vegetables
→ Daily activity
→ Less sugar and refined carbs (they push triglycerides up)
→ No smoking

Adults should get tested, and more often if heart disease runs in the family.

Fat-free means

"Fat-free" and "low-fat" on the pack — that must be the healthy choice, right? Not always.

→ Fat-free biscuits with similar calories to regular ones

label: Heatstroke danger

Body temperature of 40°C or more
with confusion or no sweating is
heatstroke — an emergency.
Cool the person and call 108.
caption:
Indian summers are getting hotter. Knowing the signs of heatstroke can save a life.

Heat exhaustion comes first:
→ Heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness
→ Headache, nausea, muscle cramps

Heatstroke is a medical emergency:
→ Body temperature 40°C (104°F) or higher
→ Confusion, slurred speech or fainting
→ Hot, dry skin — sweating may stop
→ Fast heartbeat

What to do:
→ Call 108 or 112
→ Move the person to shade or a cool room
→ Cool them fast: wet cloths, fan, cool water on skin
→ Give sips of water only if they're fully alert

Prevent it: avoid the sun from 12 to 4 PM, drink water often, and check on elderly neighbours.

Antibiotics for
a cold?

caption:
Cold, cough, sore throat — and a strip of antibiotics from the chemist? Please don't.

Most colds, flu and sore throats are caused by viruses. Antibiotics only work against bacteria.

Taking them when you don't need them:
→ Won't make you better faster
→ Can cause diarrhoea, acidity and allergic reactions
→ Upsets your gut bacteria
→ Helps create antibiotic-resistant bacteria — a serious and growing problem in India

What helps a cold:
→ Rest and fluids
→ Steam and warm salt-water gargles
→ Honey for cough (not for babies under 1)

Take antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them — and finish the course as told.

label: Did you know
headline:
Your liver can
regrow.
body: The liver can regenerate after injury — even from a partial transplant. But long-term damage from alcohol or fatty liver leaves scars.
caption:
Your liver is the only organ that can regrow lost tissue. It's remarkable — but it has limits.

That's why living-donor liver transplants work: both the donor's and the recipient's liver pieces grow back towards full size.

Your liver handles over 500 jobs, including:
→ Filtering toxins and medicines
→ Storing energy
→ Making proteins that help blood clot
→ Processing fat

But repeated damage — from alcohol, fatty liver, or hepatitis — can cause scarring (cirrhosis) that doesn't heal.

Protect it:
→ Limit or avoid alcohol
→ Keep a healthy waist size
→ Get vaccinated for hepatitis B
→ Don't overuse painkillers or unknown supplements

Phones are the easiest way to keep a toddler quiet. But young brains need something else.

→ Under 2 years: no screen time (video calls with family are fine)
→ 2 to 4 years: no more than 1 hour a day — less is better

→ Active play, several times a day
→ Talking, singing and reading with adults

→ No screens during meals

Spot a
stroke FAST

sections.text: Drooping on one side when smiling.

sections.title: Arms
sections.text: One arm weak or drifting down.

sections.title: Speech

In a stroke, brain cells die every minute without blood supply. Fast action saves lives and function.

→ A — Arms: can they raise both arms? Does one drift down?
→ S — Speech: is it slurred or strange?
→ T — Time: call 108 or 112 immediately

Other sudden signs:
→ Loss of balance or dizziness
→ Sudden blurred or lost vision
→ Severe headache with no known cause

Note the time symptoms started — doctors need it.

Don't wait for symptoms to pass. Don't give food or water. Get to a hospital with a stroke unit.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Microwaving kills
nutrients?
body: All cooking changes nutrients. Microwaving is quick and uses little water, so it often keeps more vitamins than long boiling. Use safe containers.
caption:
Some people avoid microwaves because they "destroy nutrients". It's actually one of the gentler ways to cook.

Every cooking method affects nutrients. The biggest losses happen with:
→ Long cooking times
→ High heat
→ Lots of water (vitamins leach out when you drain it)

→ Food and waste still in your gut
→ Hormones and the menstrual cycle
→ A hard workout (muscles hold water while they repair)

caption:
ORS is one of the cheapest life-saving treatments in the world. But it has to be made correctly.

Diarrhoea and vomiting drain water and salts from your body fast — especially in children and older adults.

How to make ORS:
→ Wash your hands
→ Pour one full sachet into 1 litre of clean drinking water
→ Stir until fully dissolved
→ Sip small amounts often
→ Throw away what's left after 24 hours

Shaving makes hair

caption:
"Don't shave, it'll grow back thicker." Generations have believed this one.

Shaving cuts the hair at the skin's surface. It doesn't touch the follicle under the skin, which decides how thick, dark and fast your hair grows.

Why it seems thicker:
→ A shaved hair has a blunt tip, so it feels coarse
→ New hair hasn't been lightened by the sun yet
→ Short stubble stands straighter and is more visible

Shaving tips:
→ Use a sharp, clean razor
→ Shave after a bath, when hair is soft
→ Go with the direction of hair growth to reduce bumps

→ Very high doses of supplements, without enough water

Sleep runs in cycles of roughly
90 minutes: light, deep, then REM.
A full night has 4–6 of them.
Cut sleep short, lose the later ones.
caption:
Sleep isn't one long block. It's a series of cycles, each about 90 minutes long.

Each cycle moves through:
→ Light sleep — the transition
→ Deep sleep — body repair, immune function, growth
→ REM sleep — dreaming, memory and emotions

Early in the night, cycles have more deep sleep. Later cycles have more REM.

What that means:
→ A full night gives you 4–6 cycles
→ Cutting sleep short from 7.5 to 5.5 hours mainly costs you REM
→ Waking at the end of a cycle often feels easier than waking in deep sleep

caption:
"Part of a complete breakfast." Many breakfast cereals are closer to dessert.

Plenty of popular cereals — especially chocolate, honey and "kids" ones — contain 25–35 g of sugar per 100 g, with little protein or fibre.

→ Hunger again by mid-morning
→ Cravings later in the day

→ Sugar under 10 g per 100 g
→ Fibre over 6 g per 100 g
→ Whole grain as the first ingredient

headline:
Snoring?
Don't ignore it

caption:
Loud snoring is often a family joke. Sometimes it's a sign of a serious sleep disorder.

Obstructive sleep apnoea happens when your airway repeatedly closes during sleep. Breathing stops for seconds at a time, many times a night.

Warning signs:
→ Loud, regular snoring
→ Pauses in breathing, choking or gasping (often noticed by a partner)
→ Waking up tired even after a full night
→ Morning headaches
→ Falling asleep during the day — even while driving

It's linked to high blood pressure, heart disease, diabetes and accidents.

→ Losing weight if overweight
→ Avoiding alcohol before bed
→ Sleeping on your side

Pink salt is
healthier?

Switching to Himalayan pink salt, sendha namak or sea salt for health? The difference is mostly colour.

All these salts are mostly sodium chloride — around 98% or more.

→ Most rock and pink salts are not iodised
→ Iodine is vital for your thyroid and, in pregnancy, for the baby's brain
→ India fixed widespread iodine deficiency with iodised salt

Smarter salt habits:
→ Use iodised salt for everyday cooking
→ Keep the total under 5 g a day

label: Did you know
headline:
Cooled rice has
resistant starch.
body: Cooking then cooling rice or potatoes turns some starch into resistant starch, which digests slowly and feeds gut bacteria. Refrigerate promptly.
caption:
Last night's rice may be gentler on your blood sugar than freshly cooked rice.

When starchy foods like rice, potatoes and pasta are cooked and then cooled, some of the starch changes structure. It becomes "resistant starch".

What resistant starch does:
→ Resists digestion, so it acts more like fibre
→ Feeds your good gut bacteria
→ Can lead to a smaller blood sugar rise

Reheating doesn't fully undo it.

Food safety matters with rice:
→ Cool cooked rice quickly and refrigerate within 1–2 hours
→ Eat it within a day
→ Reheat until steaming hot, only once

It's a small effect, not a magic trick. Portion size still matters most.

on face, neck and hands outdoors.
Two finger lengths for the face.
Reapply every 2 hours in the sun.

Sunscreen isn't only for beach holidays — or only for fair skin.

UV rays cause sunburn, dark spots, uneven tone and early wrinkles. Long-term, they raise the risk of skin cancer.

→ Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher
→ About two finger lengths for face and neck
→ Apply 15 minutes before going out
→ Reapply every 2 hours outdoors, and after sweating or swimming
→ Don't forget ears, neck and the backs of hands

Add shade, hats and sunglasses between 11 AM and 3 PM.

Daily sunscreen is the most proven anti-ageing product there is.

Diabetes comes
only from sugar?

caption:
"I don't eat sweets, so I can't get diabetes." Unfortunately, it's not that simple.

Type 2 diabetes develops when your body stops responding well to insulin (insulin resistance) and can't make enough to keep up.

What drives it:
→ Excess fat, especially around the belly and liver
→ Physical inactivity
→ Family history and genetics — South Asians are at higher risk
→ Large portions of refined carbs, not just sweets
→ Poor sleep and chronic stress

Sugary foods and drinks add to the risk, but they're one part of the picture.

What lowers your risk:
→ Daily movement and strength training
→ A smaller waist
→ More fibre, protein and vegetables
→ Regular check-ups after 30

Window glass

→ Midday sun makes vitamin D fastest (but avoid burning)
→ Foods: eggs, fatty fish, fortified milk

Your kidneys
filter 180 L.
body: Every day your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid from your blood, keeping what you need and making 1–2 litres of urine.
caption:
Two fist-sized organs filter your blood around the clock.

Every day, your kidneys filter about 180 litres of fluid from your blood. They return almost all of it, and turn the rest into 1–2 litres of urine.

They also:
→ Balance salt, water and minerals
→ Help control blood pressure
→ Signal your body to make red blood cells
→ Activate vitamin D

→ Keep blood sugar and BP in check
→ Drink enough water
→ Don't overuse painkillers

Kidney disease is silent until late. Test early.

Muscle turns

body: Muscle and fat are different tissues — one can't become the other. Stop training and muscle shrinks; keep eating the same and fat grows.
caption:
"If you stop going to the gym, all that muscle will turn to fat." It's a common belief — and biologically impossible.

Muscle and fat are completely different types of tissue. One can't transform into the other.

What actually happens when people stop training:
→ Muscles shrink from less use
→ They burn fewer calories through activity
→ But often keep eating the same amount
→ So fat increases

That's why it looks like muscle "turned into" fat.

How to avoid it:
→ Keep some strength training, even once or twice a week
→ Adjust portions if you're less active
→ Stay active daily

Muscle is easier to keep than to build.

Your 45-minute workout matters. But what you do in the other 23 hours may matter more for your calorie burn.

NEAT — non-exercise activity thermogenesis — is the energy you use for everything that isn't formal exercise:
→ Walking around the house or office
→ Standing instead of sitting
→ Cooking, cleaning, carrying shopping
→ Taking the stairs
→ Even fidgeting

Research shows NEAT can differ by hundreds of calories a day between people — often more than a workout burns.

Easy ways to raise it:
→ Walk during phone calls
→ Stand up every 30 minutes
→ Do your own chores
→ Use the stairs

Move more, all day.

label: Myth buster
headline:
Cracking knuckles
causes arthritis?
body: The pop is a gas bubble in the joint fluid. Studies haven't linked habitual knuckle cracking to arthritis. Pain or swelling is different.
caption:
"Stop cracking your knuckles — you'll get arthritis!" Most of us were told this as kids.

The good news: research hasn't found a link.

That popping sound comes from a gas bubble forming in the fluid that cushions your joints when you stretch them.

Studies comparing habitual knuckle crackers with non-crackers found no higher rates of arthritis. One doctor even cracked the knuckles of only one hand for 60 years — and found no difference.

When to see a doctor:
→ Pain when a joint cracks
→ Swelling or stiffness
→ Reduced movement
→ Cracking after an injury

If it doesn't hurt, it's a harmless (if annoying) habit.

label: Normal oxygen level
body:
A healthy SpO2 is usually 95–100%.
Below 94% at rest, or breathless,
needs medical advice. Warm hands,
no nail polish for a good reading.
caption:
Many Indian homes got a pulse oximeter during the pandemic. Here's how to read it properly.

SpO2 shows how much of your blood's haemoglobin is carrying oxygen.

What the numbers mean:
→ 95–100% — normal for most healthy people
→ 94% or below at rest — talk to a doctor
→ 92% or lower, or breathlessness at rest — seek urgent care

For an accurate reading:
→ Sit and rest for a few minutes
→ Warm your hands first
→ Remove nail polish or artificial nails
→ Keep your hand still and at heart level
→ Wait for the number to settle

Readings can be less accurate on darker skin. Always go by how the person feels too.

label: Reality check
headline:
Keto is the
best diet?
body: Keto can cause fast early weight loss, much of it water. Long-term, it does no better than other diets — and it's hard to stick to.
caption:
Keto promises rapid fat loss. But is it really better than other diets?

The ketogenic diet cuts carbs to very low levels — no rice, roti, fruit or dal in most versions.

What happens:
→ Fast weight loss in the first weeks — much of it water
→ Less appetite for some people
→ Hard to keep up with Indian meals and family food

Studies comparing diets over a year or more find that keto doesn't beat other approaches when calories and protein are similar.

Possible downsides:
→ Low fibre and constipation
→ Higher LDL cholesterol in some people
→ Missing out on fruit, pulses and whole grains

The best diet is one you can follow for years, not weeks.

→ Take a stair break instead of a tea break
→ Climb a few flights, several times a day

label: Did you know
headline:
Soaking dal

body: Soaking pulses for a few hours, then discarding the water, reduces gas-causing sugars and helps them cook faster. Sprouting helps even more.
caption:
Love rajma and chole but hate the bloating afterwards? How you prepare them makes a big difference.

Pulses contain certain sugars (oligosaccharides) that gut bacteria ferment — which causes gas.

Soaking helps:
→ Soak rajma, chana and other whole pulses for 8–12 hours
→ Throw away the soaking water and rinse
→ Cook in fresh water until fully soft
→ Pressure cooking helps break them down further

Other tricks:
→ Sprouting reduces gas-causing sugars even more
→ Add hing, jeera, ajwain or ginger while cooking
→ Increase pulses slowly so your gut adjusts

Don't skip pulses — they're one of the best foods for protein and fibre.

A cough lasting 2 weeks or more
can be TB. Testing and treatment
are free at government centres.
TB is curable — if treated fully.
caption:
India has the highest number of tuberculosis cases in the world. Spotting it early saves lives — and stops it spreading.

Get tested for TB if you have:
→ A cough lasting 2 weeks or more
→ Fever, especially in the evenings
→ Night sweats
→ Unexplained weight loss
→ Coughing up blood

Testing and treatment are free at government health centres under India's National TB Elimination Programme.

TB is curable. The key is to:
→ Take the full course of medicines, every day
→ Never stop when you start to feel better
→ Cover your mouth when coughing

label: Symptoms
headline:
Screen-tired
eyes?
body: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Blink more, dim glare, and keep your screen an arm's length away.
caption:
Dry, tired, burning eyes after a day of screens? It's called digital eye strain — and it's very common.

When we stare at screens, we blink much less and our eyes stay focused at one distance for hours.

The 20-20-20 rule:
→ Every 20 minutes
→ Look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away
→ For 20 seconds

Also try:
→ Blink deliberately and often
→ Keep your screen about an arm's length away, slightly below eye level
→ Match screen brightness to the room
→ Reduce glare from windows and overhead lights

See an eye doctor if symptoms continue — you may need glasses or treatment for dry eyes.

headline:
Breakfast is the
key to weight loss?
body: Studies show skipping breakfast doesn't cause weight gain, and eating it doesn't cause loss. What matters is the whole day's food quality.
caption:
"Breakfast is the most important meal of the day." For weight loss, the evidence is weaker than you'd think.

Controlled trials have found that eating breakfast doesn't automatically help people lose weight, and skipping it doesn't make them gain.

What matters more:
→ Total food across the day
→ Protein and fibre in your meals
→ Not overeating later because you're starving

Breakfast is a great idea if:
→ You're hungry in the morning
→ It keeps you from snacking on junk mid-morning
→ You have diabetes and your doctor recommends regular meals
→ You're a growing child or teen

→ It doesn't fill you up
→ It hits your blood sugar fast

→ Packaged fruit juices

label: Reality check
headline:
Painkillers are
harmless?
body: Frequent use of common painkillers can hurt your stomach, kidneys and liver, and even cause more headaches. Follow the dose and ask a doctor.
caption:
Popping a painkiller for every headache, backache or period pain? Over-the-counter doesn't mean risk-free.

Common painkillers can cause harm when used often or in high doses:
→ NSAIDs (like ibuprofen, diclofenac): stomach ulcers, acidity, kidney damage, raised BP
→ Paracetamol: liver damage if you take too much, especially with alcohol
→ Any painkiller used for headaches on many days a month can cause "rebound" headaches

Use them safely:
→ Never exceed the dose on the label
→ Check combination cold and flu medicines — they may contain the same drug
→ Take NSAIDs with food
→ Avoid them if you have kidney disease or stomach ulcers, unless a doctor says so

Needing them often? Find the cause with a doctor.

An iron kadhai

Grandma's heavy iron kadhai wasn't just tradition. It may have been adding iron to the family's food.

Studies show that cooking in cast-iron cookware can increase the iron content of food — especially acidic, moist dishes like tomato-based curries, sambar and dal, cooked for longer.

→ Season your kadhai well and dry it fully to prevent rust
→ Use it regularly for sabzis and dals
→ Don't store food in it overnight
→ Combine with vitamin C (lemon, tomato, amla) for better absorption

Walking at about 100 steps a min
is moderate intensity for most
adults. Count your steps for 15 sec,
then multiply by 4.
caption:
Is your walk actually exercise — or a stroll? There's a simple way to tell.

Research shows that walking at about 100 steps per minute counts as moderate-intensity activity for most adults — the kind that counts towards WHO's 150 minutes a week.

How to check:
→ Count your steps for 15 seconds
→ Multiply by 4
→ 100 or more = moderate pace

Another test: you can talk, but not sing.

Ways to pick up the pace:
→ Shorter, quicker steps
→ Swing your arms
→ Walk to an upbeat playlist
→ Add a slight uphill

label: Women's health
headline:
Menopause:
what helps
body: Hot flushes, poor sleep and mood swings are common. Strength training, protein, calcium and sleep help. Ask a doctor about options.
caption:
Menopause is a natural stage of life, usually between 45 and 55. Many women go through it without much support or information.

Common symptoms:
→ Hot flushes and night sweats
→ Trouble sleeping
→ Mood changes, anxiety, low mood
→ Joint aches and weight gain around the belly
→ Vaginal dryness

After menopause, bone loss speeds up and heart disease risk rises.

What helps:
→ Strength training to protect bones and muscle
→ Protein and calcium-rich foods; check vitamin D
→ Regular sleep routine, cool bedroom
→ Limiting alcohol and caffeine
→ Talking to a doctor about treatments, including hormone therapy where suitable

You don't have to just put up with it.

Coffee and chai

caption:
"Tea and coffee don't count — they dehydrate you." Not quite.

Caffeine has a mild diuretic effect, meaning it can make you pass a little more urine.

But a cup of chai or coffee is mostly water. Studies show that for regular drinkers, moderate amounts hydrate you about as well as water.

What to keep in mind:
→ Moderate is key: up to about 400 mg caffeine a day for most adults
→ Watch the sugar — 2 teaspoons a cup adds up
→ Late-day caffeine can hurt your sleep
→ Plain water is still the best main drink

label: Hb cutoff, g/dL
body:
WHO: haemoglobin below 12 g/dL in
women and 13 in men means anaemia.
In pregnancy, the cutoff is 11.
A CBC test shows your level.
caption:
Feeling tired all the time? Your haemoglobin number could explain it.

Haemoglobin (Hb) is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.

WHO defines anaemia as:
→ Below 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women
→ Below 13 g/dL in men
→ Below 11 g/dL in pregnancy

A complete blood count (CBC) is a cheap, common test that shows your Hb.

If it's low, your doctor may check:
→ Iron and ferritin
→ Vitamin B12 and folate
→ Other causes, like blood loss or worms

Treatment depends on the cause — don't start iron tablets on your own without testing.

→ Body composition

→ Whether you're holding the handrails

→ Track trends in effort, distance and heart rate
→ Compare your own workouts over time
→ Don't plan meals around the number

Protein burns
calories to digest.

caption:
Not all calories behave the same once you eat them.

Your body uses energy to digest food. This is called the thermic effect of food.

Roughly:
→ Protein: 20–30% of its calories are used just to digest it
→ Carbs: about 5–10%
→ Fat: about 0–3%

Protein also:
→ Keeps you fuller for longer
→ Helps you keep muscle while losing fat
→ Reduces cravings for many people

That's why high-protein eating is so helpful for weight management.

The low-fat craze of the 1990s taught us to fear all fat. It didn't make people healthier.

Exercise lifts

→ Yoga

→ Gives a sense of achievement

label: AQI: train indoors
body:
When the AQI crosses 200 (poor),
move workouts indoors. Above 300,
limit time outside, especially kids,
elders and those with asthma.
caption:
Winter in north India often means hazy skies and toxic air. Here's how to keep exercising without hurting your lungs.

India's Air Quality Index (AQI):
→ 0–100: good to satisfactory
→ 101–200: moderate — sensitive people take care
→ 201–300: poor — move workouts indoors
→ 301–400: very poor — limit time outside
→ 401+: severe — stay indoors as much as possible

During exercise, you breathe faster and deeper, pulling more pollution into your lungs.

A nightcap to help you sleep? It may knock you out — but it ruins the sleep that follows.

→ Sleep becomes lighter and more broken
→ You wake up more often, especially in the second half of the night
→ REM sleep — important for memory and mood — is reduced

caption:
Dengue season is here. Most cases are mild — but knowing the danger signs can save a life.

Typical dengue: sudden high fever, severe body and joint pain, headache, pain behind the eyes, and sometimes a rash.

The risky phase often comes around days 3–7, as the fever starts to drop.

Go to a hospital immediately if you see:
→ Severe stomach pain or repeated vomiting
→ Bleeding from gums or nose, or blood in vomit or stool
→ Fast breathing
→ Extreme tiredness, restlessness or confusion
→ Cold, clammy skin

What to do:
→ Rest and drink plenty of fluids — ORS, water, soups
→ Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen or aspirin unless a doctor advises
→ Prevent bites: no standing water, nets, full sleeves

Don't wait it out.

caption:
Men, if you're getting up several times a night to pee, don't just blame age.

The prostate is a small gland below the bladder. As men age, it commonly enlarges, which can squeeze the urine tube.

Signs to watch for:
→ Waking up at night to urinate, often
→ A weak or interrupted stream
→ Trouble starting
→ Feeling the bladder isn't empty
→ Urgency or dribbling

Most of the time it's benign prostatic enlargement, which is very treatable.

But see a doctor promptly if you have:
→ Blood in urine or semen
→ Pain while urinating
→ Bone pain or unexplained weight loss

Sleep locks in

Overthinking?

caption:
Do worries follow you around all day — and into bed at night? Try giving them an appointment.

"Worry time" is a technique used in cognitive behavioural therapy.

How it works:
→ Pick a set 15-minute slot every day — early evening, not just before bed
→ During the day, when a worry pops up, write it down in a few words
→ Tell yourself: "I'll think about this at worry time"
→ At worry time, go through the list. Problem-solve what you can
→ When time's up, close the notebook

Many people find that by worry time, half the worries no longer matter.

→ Rest and sleep

→ Rotating with vegetable oils like mustard, groundnut or rice bran

Light sets your

caption:
Nearly 1 in 3 adults worldwide isn't moving enough. In India, the numbers are even higher.

WHO reported that in 2022, 31% of adults — about 1.8 billion people — didn't meet the recommended 150 minutes of activity a week.

→ Heart disease and stroke
→ Type 2 diabetes
→ Some cancers

Getting started is simpler than you think:
→ A 10-minute walk after each meal

Longer workouts
are always better?

Spending two hours at the gym, half of it on your phone? Longer isn't always better.

For most people, a focused 30–45 minute workout can deliver most of the strength and fitness benefits.

What matters more than time:
→ Consistency — 3–4 sessions a week, every week
→ Effort — working close to your limit on strength sets
→ Progress — gradually adding weight, reps or intensity
→ Recovery — sleep and rest days

Make short workouts count:
→ Have a plan before you walk in
→ Focus on big movements: squats, push-ups, rows, lunges
→ Keep rest times reasonable
→ Phone on airplane mode

label: Women's health
headline:
Prevent
UTIs
body: Drink enough fluids, pee when you need to, and after sex. Wipe front to back. Burning, urgency or fever means see a doctor.
caption:
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are very common in women — and painful. A few habits lower the risk.

Common signs:
→ Burning while passing urine
→ Needing to go often and urgently
→ Cloudy or strong-smelling urine
→ Lower belly pain

Prevention tips:
→ Drink enough water through the day
→ Don't hold in urine for long — common at work or while travelling
→ Pee after sex
→ Wipe front to back
→ Wear breathable cotton underwear
→ Avoid harsh soaps or douches in the genital area

See a doctor — don't self-medicate with leftover antibiotics.

Fever, back pain or blood in urine? Seek care quickly — it may have reached the kidneys.

headline:
Your gut lining
renews in days.
body: Cells lining your intestines are replaced every few days — some of the fastest renewal in your body. Fibre and good food help it.
caption:
Some of the busiest cells in your body line your gut.

The cells lining your intestines are replaced every few days. It's one of the fastest-renewing tissues in the body.

Why? They face constant wear from food, acid, enzymes and bacteria.

What supports a healthy gut lining:
→ Fibre — it feeds gut bacteria that make compounds the lining cells use for energy
→ A variety of plant foods
→ Fermented foods like curd
→ Limiting alcohol
→ Not overusing painkillers like NSAIDs, which can irritate the gut
→ Managing stress and sleeping well

Your gut rebuilds itself constantly. Give it the right materials.

Tobacco is one of India's biggest health problems — and it's completely preventable.

label: Heart health
headline:
Habits that
lower BP

sections.title: Less salt
sections.text: Under 5 g a day; skip pickles, papad.

sections.title: Move
sections.text: 30 min brisk walking, most days.

sections.title: Also
sections.text: Lose belly fat, sleep well, limit alcohol.

caption:
High blood pressure? Lifestyle changes can lower it meaningfully — sometimes as much as a medicine.

What works:
→ Cut salt to under 5 g a day — less pickle, papad, namkeen and packaged food
→ More fruit, vegetables, dal and low-fat dairy
→ 30 minutes of brisk walking on most days
→ Lose weight if you carry extra, especially around the belly
→ Limit or avoid alcohol
→ Quit tobacco
→ Sleep 7–8 hours and manage stress

Each change can lower BP by a few points. Together, they add up.

Important: if your doctor has prescribed BP medicine, don't stop it on your own. Make the changes, monitor your BP, and review with your doctor.

"Don't let kids lift weights — it'll stunt their growth." This old myth keeps many children away from a healthy activity.

high-quality protein, plus B12,
vitamin D and choline. Two eggs at

Looking for an affordable, easy protein? The humble egg is hard to beat.

One large egg provides about 6 g of high-quality protein — with all the essential amino acids your body needs.

It also gives you:
→ Vitamin B12
→ Vitamin D (one of the few food sources)
→ Choline, important for the brain

→ Egg bhurji with vegetables
→ A vegetable omelette with whole wheat toast
→ Egg curry with roti

label: Reality check
headline:
Cholesterol is only
an old-age issue?
body: High cholesterol can start in your 20s, and some families inherit very high levels. Get a lipid profile in your 20s and repeat it regularly.
caption:
"I'm too young to worry about cholesterol." Plaque in your arteries starts building decades before a heart attack.

High cholesterol has no symptoms. You can feel fine and still have high levels.

Who should pay attention early:
→ Anyone with a family history of early heart attacks (men before 55, women before 65)
→ People with diabetes, high BP or excess belly fat
→ Smokers
→ Anyone who hasn't ever been tested

Some families have a genetic condition — familial hypercholesterolaemia — that causes very high LDL from birth.

What to do:
→ Get a lipid profile in your 20s
→ Repeat every few years, or as your doctor advises
→ Build heart-healthy habits now

It's easier to prevent than to reverse.

label: Gut health
headline:
Fibre without
the bloat
body: Jumping from low to high fibre overnight causes gas. Add one serving every few days, drink more water, and let your gut adjust.
caption:
Started eating more fibre and now feel bloated and gassy? You probably went too fast.

Your gut bacteria need time to adjust to more fibre. A sudden jump can cause gas, bloating and discomfort.

How to increase fibre comfortably:
→ Add one extra serving every few days, not all at once
→ Drink more water alongside — fibre needs fluid
→ Cook pulses well; soak them first
→ Start with gentler options: oats, cooked vegetables, fruit like papaya and banana
→ Then add rajma, chana, raw salads and more whole grains
→ Stay active — movement helps digestion

Most people feel the bloating settle within a few weeks.

The goal: around 25–30 g of fibre a day.

label: Did you know
headline:
Spinach isn't an
iron superstar.
body: Spinach contains iron, but oxalates block much of it from being absorbed. Still eat it — and pair greens with vitamin C, dal and other iron sources.
caption:
Spinach has a reputation as the ultimate iron food. It's more complicated than that.

Spinach does contain iron, but it also contains oxalates — compounds that bind to iron and calcium and block much of it from being absorbed.

Plant iron in general is less easily absorbed than iron from meat, fish and eggs.

Better ways to boost iron:
→ Combine iron-rich foods with vitamin C: lemon on palak dal, amla, guava
→ Eat a variety: dal, rajma, chana, ragi, bajra, sesame, jaggery in small amounts
→ For non-vegetarians: eggs, fish, chicken, meat
→ Keep chai and coffee away from meals

Spinach is still great — for fibre, folate, vitamin K and more. Just don't rely on it alone for iron.

label: Normal bowel range
body:
Anything from 3 times a day to
3 times a week can be normal.
What matters is a change from
your usual — and how it feels.

How often should you go to the toilet? There's a wider range of normal than most people think.

→ No straining or pain
→ A pattern that's normal for you

→ A lasting change from your usual pattern
→ Blood in stool, or black, tarry stools
→ Unexplained weight loss

→ Pain that wakes you at night

Sunday night
dread?

caption:
Sunday evening comes and your stomach sinks thinking about Monday? The "Sunday scaries" are very common.

What helps:
→ On Friday, write down your top 3 tasks for Monday — your brain can let go over the weekend
→ Prepare small things on Saturday, not Sunday night: clothes, tiffin plan, bag
→ Plan something enjoyable for Sunday evening — a walk, a call, a favourite meal
→ Keep Sunday's bedtime and wake-up time close to weekdays
→ Limit checking work emails on weekends

If the dread is intense every week, notice what's driving it:
→ Workload?
→ A difficult manager or colleague?
→ The job itself?

label: Myth buster
headline:
Sugar feeds
cancer?
body: All cells use glucose. Eating sugar doesn't directly make cancer grow, but excess sugar drives weight gain, which raises cancer risk.
caption:
"Sugar feeds cancer, so cut it out completely." This message spreads widely, especially among worried families.

Here's what the science says:
→ Every cell in your body uses glucose for energy — including cancer cells
→ Your body makes glucose even if you eat no sugar at all
→ There's no evidence that eating sugar directly makes cancer grow faster

The real link:
→ A diet high in sugar can lead to weight gain
→ Excess body fat raises the risk of at least 13 types of cancer

For people with cancer, extreme diets can cause dangerous weight and muscle loss. Always follow the advice of the cancer care team.

Limit added sugar for overall health — not out of fear.

Teenagers aren't just being "moody". Many are struggling with real mental health conditions.

WHO estimates that about 1 in 7 young people aged 10–19 experience a mental disorder. Half of all mental health conditions start by age 14 — but most go undetected and untreated.

Signs to watch for in teens:
→ Withdrawing from friends and family
→ Big changes in sleep or appetite
→ Falling grades or skipping school
→ Constant irritability, sadness or worry
→ Talking about feeling hopeless

label: Reality check
headline:
Cardio kills your
muscle gains?
body: For most people, adding cardio barely affects muscle growth. Only very high amounts may interfere. Cardio boosts recovery and heart health.
caption:
Avoiding all cardio because you're afraid of losing your hard-earned muscle? You don't need to.

Research shows that for most people, combining cardio with strength training has little impact on muscle growth.

Only very high amounts of endurance training — like marathon training while trying to bulk up — may interfere.

Cardio actually helps lifters:
→ A stronger heart and better recovery between sets
→ Better blood sugar and cholesterol
→ More stamina for longer sessions

How to combine them:
→ Do strength training first if both are on the same day
→ Or split them — e.g., morning cardio, evening lifting
→ Walking and cycling are easy on recovery
→ Eat enough protein

You don't have to choose between strong and fit.

Try exercise

No time for a full workout? Try "exercise snacks" — short bursts of activity spread through your day.

→ A brisk walk around the building

label: Did you know
headline:
Thirst fades
with age.
body: Older adults often feel less thirsty even when they need water, which raises the risk of dehydration. Offer drinks regularly, not just when asked.
caption:
Grandparents saying "I'm not thirsty" doesn't mean they're well hydrated.

As we age, the body's thirst signal weakens. Older adults can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty.

Other factors add to the risk:
→ Some medicines, like diuretics
→ Avoiding drinks to reduce toilet trips
→ Hot Indian summers
→ Illness, fever or diarrhoea

Signs of dehydration in older adults:
→ Confusion or unusual drowsiness
→ Dizziness or falls
→ Dark urine, or less of it
→ Constipation
→ Dry mouth

How to help:
→ Offer water, buttermilk, soups and fruits through the day
→ Keep a water bottle within reach
→ Set gentle reminders

Small sips, often.
